title: Spondylolisthesis (Slipped Vertebra): Do I Need Spinal Fusion?
seoTitle: Spondylolisthesis: Do You Need Spinal Fusion?
metaDescription: Spondylolisthesis means one vertebra has slipped forward. Most people improve without surgery. Learn when surgery helps and when fusion is added.
intro: Being told that a bone in your back has "slipped" can sound alarming, and many people assume it means an operation with screws and rods. In most cases it does not. This article explains what spondylolisthesis is, how it is usually treated, and when surgery, with or without fusion, is worth discussing.
summary: Spondylolisthesis means one vertebra has slipped forward over the one below, usually in the lower back. Many people have mild symptoms or none at all, and most are treated with exercise, physiotherapy and medicines. Surgery is considered when leg pain or weakness persists despite good non-operative care. Fusion is not always needed.

sections.heading: What is spondylolisthesis, and is it the same as a slipped disc?
sections.body: Spondylolisthesis is when one vertebra (a bone of the spine) slides forward over the bone below it, most often in the lower back. It is not the same as a "slipped disc", where the soft cushion between two vertebrae bulges or ruptures and presses on a nerve. The bone itself has not moved in a slipped disc. AAOS OrthoInfo describes two common types in adults. Degenerative spondylolisthesis comes from age-related wear of the discs, joints and ligaments; it is more common in women and in people over 50, and often narrows the spinal canal (spinal stenosis). Isthmic spondylolisthesis starts with a small stress fracture in a part of the vertebra called the pars interarticularis, usually from adolescence, which may go unnoticed until adult life. Doctors grade the slip by how far the bone has moved; most adults have a low-grade (small) slip. If your problem is a disc, our article on slipped disc and sciatica is more relevant.

sections.heading: What symptoms does a slipped vertebra cause?
sections.body: Some people with spondylolisthesis have no symptoms at all; it is found by chance on an X-ray. Others have low back pain, leg pain, or a heavy, tired, numb feeling in the legs that comes on with standing or walking and eases with sitting or bending forward. According to OrthoInfo, degenerative slips typically cause leg and/or back pain with leg weakness on prolonged standing or walking, similar to lumbar spinal stenosis. Isthmic slips more often cause activity-related low back pain, sometimes with leg pain. The size of the slip on a scan does not always match how much pain you have, so treatment is guided by your symptoms and examination, not the image alone.

sections.heading: Can spondylolisthesis be treated without surgery?
sections.body: Yes. Most people are treated without surgery. Non-operative care does not move the bone back into place, but many patients find it relieves their symptoms well enough to live normally. Treatment usually combines physiotherapy and exercise, pain medicines, activity changes and, for some, a spinal injection. OrthoInfo notes that steroid injections may ease pain and numbness but usually not leg weakness, and should not be repeated more than a few times a year. It suggests reassessing after about 3 to 6 months of non-surgical care for degenerative slips, and 6 to 12 months for isthmic slips. For more on injections, see back pain injections and treatments.
bullets: Core and back-strengthening exercises guided by a physiotherapist
Short courses of pain relievers or anti-inflammatory medicines, if safe for you
Staying active within comfort rather than prolonged bed rest
Weight management and walking breaks if standing or walking brings on leg symptoms
Selected injections for nerve pain that is not settling

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body: Surgery is considered when leg pain, numbness or weakness persists and seriously limits your life despite a good trial of non-operative care, when nerve weakness is getting worse, or rarely when the slip is progressing. Back X-rays alone, without matching symptoms, are not a reason for surgery. OrthoInfo describes surgery for degenerative slips when symptoms persist after 3 to 6 months of non-surgical treatment, especially if you cannot walk or stand for long and the pain or weakness significantly affects your quality of life. For isthmic slips, it lists symptoms persisting after 6 to 12 months, worsening nerve symptoms (weakness, numbness, frequent falls) or signs of cauda equina syndrome. An MRI is usually needed before planning surgery; see do I need an MRI for back pain?

sections.heading: Decompression alone or decompression with fusion: which is right?
sections.body:
There is no single answer. Decompression removes bone spurs and thickened ligament to free the squeezed nerves. Fusion adds screws and rods to join two vertebrae so the unstable segment stops moving. Whether fusion is added depends on how stable the spine is, the type of slip and your overall health.

Two trials published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016 looked at this question. In the Swedish trial led by Försth, 247 patients with lumbar spinal stenosis, with or without degenerative spondylolisthesis, were randomised to decompression with or without fusion; as reported by Healio, outcomes at 2 and 5 years were not better with fusion. In the smaller US trial led by Ghogawala, 66 patients with a low-grade degenerative slip were randomised; adding fusion gave a slightly greater improvement in physical quality-of-life scores, and fewer patients needed repeat surgery (14% with fusion versus 34% with decompression alone). Because these results point in different directions, the decision is individual. OrthoInfo notes that if the spine is stable enough, fusion may not be needed.

sections.heading: What symptoms need urgent attention?
sections.body: Seek emergency care the same day if back or leg pain comes with new difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the genitals, buttocks or inner thighs (saddle area), or leg weakness that is getting worse. These can be signs of cauda equina syndrome or severe nerve compression, which may need urgent surgery. These situations are uncommon, but delays can lead to permanent damage. Do not wait for a routine appointment if they occur; go to the nearest emergency department or contact us immediately.
bullets: New difficulty passing urine, or leaking urine or stool
Numbness in the saddle area (between the legs, buttocks or inner thighs)
Leg weakness or foot drop that is getting worse
Severe pain with fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer

faqs.q: Is spondylolisthesis the same as a slipped disc?
faqs.a: No. In spondylolisthesis a vertebra (bone) slides forward. In a slipped disc, the soft cushion between the bones bulges and presses on a nerve. The two can cause similar leg pain but are different conditions.

faqs.q: Does every slipped vertebra need surgery?
faqs.a: No. Many people have no symptoms or improve with physiotherapy, exercise and medicines. Surgery is considered mainly for persistent leg symptoms that limit daily life despite good non-operative care, or for worsening nerve weakness.

faqs.q: Will exercises put the bone back in place?
faqs.a: No. Non-operative treatment does not reverse the slip, but it often relieves pain and improves function enough that surgery is not needed.

faqs.q: If I need surgery, will I definitely need fusion?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Trials published in 2016 gave mixed results on adding fusion to decompression. Your surgeon will consider spinal stability, the type of slip and your health before recommending decompression alone or with fusion.

faqs.q: When should I go to hospital urgently?
faqs.a: Go immediately if you develop bladder or bowel changes, numbness in the saddle area, or leg weakness that is getting worse. These can signal cauda equina syndrome.
